passage: On stream selection day, the Class 10 corridor smelled of fresh photocopies. The form had three boxes: Science, Commerce, Humanities. Preeti's pen hovered over Humanities; she'd topped history every year and filled two notebooks with essays nobody had asked for. Then she looked around. Vijay, Anu, the whole lunch group were ticking Science. "Everyone good goes science," Vijay said, not even looking up. Preeti's stomach knotted. If she ticked Humanities, she'd be in a different building next year, eating lunch with strangers, the girl who couldn't handle science. Her palms were damp. She ticked Science, folded the form quickly, and handed it to the class teacher before she could change her mind. On the way out she passed the humanities noticeboard and didn't look at it.

qa.q: Which subject had Preeti topped every year?
qa.a: She'd topped history every year.

qa.q: What do Preeti's knotted stomach and damp palms suggest?
qa.a: They suggest she felt anxious about standing out, picturing lunch with strangers and being called the girl who couldn't handle science. 😰

qa.q: What could Preeti do before the forms are finalised?
qa.a: She could talk to a teacher or parent about what she really loves and ask whether she can still change her stream.

qa.q: How might Vijay's quick 'Everyone good goes science' land for others choosing?
qa.a: Said so casually, it makes any other choice sound second-best, which can push classmates like Preeti to follow the crowd.

grounding: A teenager picks science because her whole group does, though she loves history, anxious about standing out.

passage:
Dear Leela,
You asked why I sounded so tired on the phone. It's the streak thing. In my class, everyone posts a photo of their study desk at 3 am, every night, with a counter: Day 12, Day 20. Whoever breaks the streak gets teased in the group chat. I didn't want to start. I don't even study well that late; I just stare at the page. But when the whole class was doing it and I wasn't, it felt like a spotlight on my empty square. So I started. I'm on Day 9. My eyes burn in first period, and yesterday I fell asleep on the bus and missed my stop.
I know it's silly. I just can't be the only one who stops.
Chetan

qa.q: What day of the streak is Chetan on?
qa.a: Chetan is on Day 9.

qa.q: Why did Chetan start the streak despite not studying well that late?
qa.a: With the whole class posting, Chetan felt a spotlight on the empty square and was anxious about being the only one left out.

qa.q: What could help Chetan stop without feeling alone?
qa.a: Chetan could find one or two classmates who also hate it and quit together, and tell a parent or teacher how tired it's making them.

qa.q: How might Leela feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Leela may feel worried about Chetan falling asleep on the bus, and glad to have been told the real reason for the tiredness.

grounding: A teenager joins a late-night study streak because the whole class does it and fears being the only one who stops.

passage: Nazia, you'll laugh, but I have to tell you about the shoes. In September, three girls in my section came to school in those chunky white sneakers with the thick soles. By October it was fifteen. By November, I was the only one in Class 9 B in plain black school shoes. Nobody said anything, honestly. But I felt like everyone was looking at my feet. I'm Shreya, the one who used to say trends are silly. I begged Mummy for a week. She finally bought them, and they pinch, and I actually think they look like boats. I wore them anyway, every day. And then in January, half the class switched to canvas shoes. Guess what I asked for.

qa.q: How many in Shreya's section had the chunky sneakers by October?
qa.a: By October it was fifteen.

qa.q: Why did Shreya beg for shoes that pinch and look like boats?
qa.a: Being the only one in plain black shoes made Shreya feel watched and anxious, so fitting in mattered more than comfort or taste.

qa.q: What question could Shreya ask before asking for the canvas shoes?
qa.a: Shreya could ask, 'Would I still want these if nobody in class had them?' before deciding.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the canvas shoe request after the sneakers?
qa.a: Mummy may feel frustrated or amused, having given in after a week of begging for shoes Shreya now wants to replace.

grounding: A teenager begs for the sneakers the whole section wears, despite disliking them, then chases the next trend.

passage: Damini, before you judge me, let me explain. Last March, every single guy on my hostel floor was talking about this new digital coin. Group chat, mess, even the laundry line. Forty people. Forty! I thought: forty engineering students can't all be wrong, right? I didn't read anything about it. I didn't know who made it. I just saw the number of people and the green arrows on their phones, and I put in my whole semester's pocket money. I'm Tanvir, and I once lectured you about reading terms and conditions. Anyway. It dropped to almost nothing in April. The funny thing? When I asked around, most of the forty had joined because the others had. Nobody had actually checked anything.

qa.q: How many people on Tanvir's floor were talking about the coin?
qa.a: Forty people.

qa.q: Why did Tanvir feel safe putting in the whole semester's pocket money?
qa.a: Tanvir thought forty engineering students couldn't all be wrong, so the crowd itself felt like proof.

qa.q: What would you advise Tanvir the next time something is suddenly popular?
qa.a: Find out who made it and what it actually is, and talk it over with a trusted adult before putting in money, however many have joined.

qa.q: What might Damini be thinking while listening to this?
qa.a: Damini might find it ironic, since Tanvir once lectured Damini about reading terms and conditions.

grounding: A student puts a semester's pocket money into a coin because forty hostel-mates had, treating popularity as proof.

passage: I'm Tenzin, Binita's roommate, and I watched her decide how to vote in the student council election. Two weeks before, she had a list on her desk: hostel water, library hours, the women's safety committee. She'd even read both manifestos. Then, three days before polling, the whole corridor started wearing Rakesh's yellow badges. Posters on every door. In the mess, people just said, "Everyone's voting Rakesh." Binita came back one evening with a yellow badge. When I asked what his plan for the library was, she said, "Honestly, no idea. But half the campus can't be wrong." Her list was still on the desk, and his name wasn't on it. I don't know exactly why she changed. Maybe she just didn't want to be on the losing side.

qa.q: What colour were Rakesh's badges?
qa.a: They were yellow.

qa.q: What does Binita's 'half the campus can't be wrong' suggest about her thinking?
qa.a: It suggests she was treating the number of supporters as proof, even though she didn't know his plan for the library.

qa.q: What could Binita do before polling day?
qa.a: She could check Rakesh's plans against her own list about water, library hours and safety, then vote for whoever matches it best.

qa.q: How does Tenzin see Binita's change?
qa.a: Tenzin notices the list still on the desk and wonders whether Binita just didn't want to be on the losing side.

grounding: A roommate watches a student drop her own checklist and vote for the popular candidate because everyone else is.

passage:
Monday. In the college canteen, it seemed everyone had joined the new home business group selling skincare kits. Usha's feed was full of classmates posing with boxes. "Two hundred students already," Imran said. "Can't all be fools." Usha paid the joining fee that night without reading the terms.
Thursday. The group's leader messaged: the way to earn was to bring in five friends, each paying the same fee. Usha asked what happened if the friends didn't sell anything. The leader replied with a video of people clapping.
The following Wednesday. Usha sat on the hostel bed with three unopened kits and a list of friends Usha didn't want to ask. Imran came by. "I haven't recruited anyone either," he admitted. "I don't think most of the two hundred have." Usha opened the terms and read them for the first time.

qa.q: What was the way to earn, according to the group's leader?
qa.a: The way to earn was to bring in five friends, each paying the same fee.

qa.q: Why did Usha pay without reading the terms?
qa.a: With two hundred students already in and Imran saying they can't all be fools, the popularity felt like enough proof.

qa.q: What could Usha and Imran do now?
qa.a: They could stop recruiting, read the terms together, and ask a trusted adult or the college for guidance about the fee.

qa.q: How might the friends on Usha's list feel if Usha had pushed them to join?
qa.a: They might feel pressured and used, paying a fee mainly so Usha could earn, which could strain the friendships.

grounding: A student joins a selling scheme because two hundred classmates had, and only later reads what it really is.

passage: In the Toronto office kitchen, the sign-up sheet for the city marathon had eighteen names on it. "You're the only one on the team who hasn't signed," Yosef said, grinning, pen held out. Noa took the pen, then paused. She asked herself two questions she'd started using lately: Why do I want this? And would I still do it if nobody ever knew? The honest answers were: because everyone else is, and no. She hated long runs; she loved her Saturday swims. "Not this one," she said, handing the pen back. "But I'll be at the finish line with snacks and a very loud sign." Yosef laughed. "Deal." Two weeks later she signed up for the office's open-water swim, alone on the sheet, and didn't mind at all.

qa.q: How many names were on the marathon sign-up sheet?
qa.a: The sheet had eighteen names on it.

qa.q: What did Noa realise when she answered her two questions honestly?
qa.a: She realised she only wanted to sign because everyone else had, and that she'd never run it if nobody knew, since she hated long runs.

qa.q: How did Noa stay connected to the team while saying no?
qa.a: She offered to be at the finish line with snacks and a loud sign, backing them without running a race she didn't want.

qa.q: How does Yosef react to Noa's choice?
qa.a: Yosef laughs and says 'Deal', showing Yosef accepts her choice and her offer to cheer.

grounding: A young woman checks why she wants to join a popular marathon, declines, stays connected, and later picks a swim alone.

passage: At the agricultural research institute, the new drone-mapping project was the talk of the canteen. Nine of the twelve junior scientists had already asked to move onto it. "You're joining, right?" Kishore asked Gurleen, sliding into the chair opposite. Gurleen stirred her tea. She had a habit of asking herself, before any big move: Why do I want this? And what would I pick if nobody ever knew my choice? She thought about it that evening, sketching on the back of a lab report. The answer surprised her. She did want it; she'd been curious about soil mapping for years, long before it was fashionable. The next morning she applied, and wrote exactly which part she wanted to work on. "Following the herd?" Kishore teased. "Walking with it," she said. "On purpose."

qa.q: How many junior scientists had already asked to move onto the drone project?
qa.a: Nine of the twelve junior scientists had.

qa.q: Why was Gurleen surprised by her own answer?
qa.a: She half expected to find she was just following the crowd, but found she'd been curious about soil mapping for years and really wanted it.

qa.q: What did writing exactly which part she wanted add to Gurleen's application?
qa.a: It showed her choice came from her own interest and gave her a clear role, instead of just joining a crowd.

qa.q: What does Kishore's teasing 'Following the herd?' suggest Kishore assumed?
qa.a: Kishore seems to assume she's joining because everyone else did, not knowing she had checked her own reasons first.

grounding: A young scientist asks herself why she wants to join a popular project and joins it deliberately, for her own reasons.

passage:
Dear Hrithik,
You asked if I'm moving to Bengaluru like everyone else. Pankaj left in March, then Rupal, then half my college group. My phone is full of their new office photos. For a month I kept opening job sites at midnight.
Then I did what Mummy taught us: I asked myself why I wanted it. Honestly, mostly so I wouldn't feel left behind. Then I asked what I'd choose if none of them would ever find out. That one was easy. I'd stay in Indore, keep teaching at the school, and finish my B.Ed.
So I'm staying, on purpose this time, not because I'm scared to go. If one day I want Bengaluru for my own reasons, I'll go then.
Your didi,
Sunita

qa.q: What would Sunita choose if none of the friends would ever find out?
qa.a: She'd stay in Indore, keep teaching at the school, and finish her B.Ed.

qa.q: Why did Sunita keep opening job sites at midnight?
qa.a: With half her college group posting office photos, she felt left behind and anxious to keep up.

qa.q: What makes Sunita's decision deliberate rather than fearful?
qa.a: She checked both her reason for wanting to go and what she'd choose in private, and left the door open to go later for her own reasons.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel reading Sunita didi's answer?
qa.a: Hrithik may feel reassured that she's staying by choice, and maybe pick up a way to make Hrithik's own decisions. 🙂

grounding: A young teacher asks why she wants to follow friends to a new city and what she'd pick privately, then stays on purpose.

subtype: Teacher or elder is always right [Actor]
passage:
"Didi, spiders are insects. Vasudha Ma'am said so."
Pooja looked up from her book. "Om, spiders have eight legs. Insects have six. It's right here in your own science book."
"But Ma'am said insects."
"Maybe she made a small mistake."
"Teachers don't make mistakes." Om's voice got smaller. "And if I say anything, she'll look at me with that face."
"What face?"
"The one where everyone goes quiet."
"You could just ask, 'Ma'am, the book says eight legs, can you explain?'"
Om shook his head hard. "No. I'll write insects. She's the teacher."
"Even if the book says eight legs?"
"She knows more than the book." He crossed out the right word in his notebook and wrote "insect", pressing hard.

qa.q: How many legs does Pooja say spiders have?
qa.a: Pooja says spiders have eight legs.

qa.q: Why does Om refuse to ask Vasudha Ma'am about the eight legs?
qa.a: He is scared of 'that face' where everyone goes quiet, and he believes teachers don't make mistakes, so respect and fear are mixed together.

qa.q: How could Pooja help Om feel safe to check the fact?
qa.a: She could practise the polite question with him at home, or suggest he show Ma'am the textbook page quietly after class.

qa.q: How might Vasudha Ma'am feel if Om asked his question kindly?
qa.a: She might be glad he read his book so carefully and happily fix the slip, since most teachers want their students to get it right.

grounding: A boy writes that spiders are insects because his teacher said so, even when his own book says otherwise, too afraid to ask.

passage: I'm Uday, and this happened at Ammamma's house last summer. Harsha Mama is the cleverest person in our family; he's an engineer and everyone asks him things. At dinner he said a heavy stone always falls faster than a light one. I nearly said something. In school, Revathi Miss had shown us: she dropped a big stone and a small stone from the first-floor balcony, and they hit the ground together. I saw it with my own eyes. But Mama said it so surely, and all the grown-ups nodded. My face went hot. So I nodded too, and Ammamma patted my head. "Good boy, listen to Mama." That night I lay awake thinking: I saw it. But Mama is Mama.

qa.q: What did Revathi Miss drop from the first-floor balcony?
qa.a: She dropped a big stone and a small stone, and they hit the ground together.

qa.q: Why did Uday nod even after seeing the stones land together?
qa.a: Harsha Mama spoke so surely and all the grown-ups nodded, so Uday feared looking foolish, and respect for Mama outweighed his own eyes.

qa.q: How could Uday bring up what he saw without being rude?
qa.a: He could say, 'Mama, in school we tried it and they landed together. Can we try it tomorrow?' and test it together.

qa.q: How might Harsha Mama react if Uday showed him the stones?
qa.a: As an engineer, Mama might be curious and pleased that Uday remembered the experiment, even if it proves him wrong.

grounding: A boy agrees with his uncle that heavy stones fall faster, despite seeing otherwise, because the elder sounded sure.

subtype: Teacher or elder is always right [Actor]
passage:
Tuition notes, Gargi, Tuesday
Tarun, age 9, came in today with his maths homework. Every answer in the 8 times table was right except 7 × 8, where he had written 54. I asked him to count it out with beads. He got 56, twice. Then he said quietly, "But Neelam Ma'am wrote 54 on the board." I asked if the board might be wrong. He looked frightened and whispered, "Ma'am is never wrong. If I write 56 she'll be angry." He wanted to keep 54.
What I did: I told him that checking is brave and respectful, and that teachers are glad when children notice slips. We practised saying, "Ma'am, I counted 56. Could you check?" He wrote 56 in pencil next to the 54. I've also sent a short, friendly note to Neelam Ma'am.

qa.q: What had Tarun written for 7 × 8?
qa.a: He had written 54.

qa.q: What does Tarun's frightened whisper suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels questioning his teacher would bring anger, and that his trust in her is mixed with fear.

qa.q: How did Gargi help Tarun without making him disrespect his teacher?
qa.a: Gargi let him count with beads, practised a polite question with him, and sent a friendly note to Neelam Ma'am.

qa.q: How might Neelam Ma'am feel when she gets Gargi's note?
qa.a: She would probably be glad to fix the slip, and may realise some children are too scared to point out mistakes.

grounding: A tutor notes a boy keeping a wrong answer because his teacher wrote it, too afraid to question her.

passage: At volleyball practice in São Paulo, Coach Ramos watched Priscila set the ball and shook his head. "Left-handers can't be setters. Never works. Go back to the outside." He had coached for twenty years and said it like a fact. Priscila jogged back, cheeks burning. That night she couldn't stop thinking about it. Twenty years was a lot of years. But her friend Jana had shown her videos of a left-handed setter in the national league, and Priscila's own sets had landed well all week. The next day, stomach fluttering, she stayed after practice. "Coach, can I ask something? I found a left-handed setter in the national league. Could I try for two weeks?" Coach Ramos frowned for a long moment. "Two weeks," he said. "Then we see." She walked out feeling both stupid and brave.

qa.q: How long had Coach Ramos coached?
qa.a: He had coached for twenty years.

qa.q: Why did Priscila feel both stupid and brave walking out?
qa.a: Questioning a coach with twenty years' experience felt awkward and embarrassing, but she trusted the evidence enough to ask anyway.

qa.q: What made Priscila's question respectful?
qa.a: She asked privately after practice, brought a real example, and asked for a short trial instead of telling him he was wrong.

qa.q: How might Coach Ramos see Priscila's question?
qa.a: He might feel challenged at first, as his long frown shows, but respect her effort enough to give her two weeks.

grounding: A teenager weighs a sure-sounding coach's claim against evidence and, awkwardly, asks to test it.

passage: In the packed auditorium of the coaching centre, the director, introduced as "a gold medallist and national topper", told three hundred students, "If you sleep much at all, forget about the entrance exam." Pens scratched. Saurabh wrote it down too, then hesitated. Just last week the school's biology teacher had said teenagers need plenty of sleep to remember what they learn. Two sure voices, two different answers. After the talk, Saurabh caught Sonali by the water cooler. "Do you believe the no-sleep thing?" "He's a national topper," she said. "But is being a topper the same as knowing about sleep?" Saurabh asked, and immediately felt silly. Sonali paused. "Hm. Maybe ask Ma'am again?" He crossed out the note, then half rewrote it in pencil, just in case.

qa.q: How was the director introduced?
qa.a: As a gold medallist and national topper.

qa.q: Why did Saurabh feel silly after asking his question?
qa.a: Doubting a national topper in front of Sonali felt awkward, even though he suspected being a topper isn't the same as knowing about sleep.

qa.q: What is a good next step for Saurabh?
qa.a: He could go back to the biology teacher, whose view is the one to check with here, and look at where each claim comes from rather than trusting whoever sounds most impressive.

qa.q: Why might Sonali lean on the director's title at first?
qa.a: A confident speaker with a big title can feel safer to trust than her own doubt, though her pause shows she starts to question it too.

grounding: A teenager weighs a titled speaker's confident claim against a teacher's and awkwardly starts questioning whether titles guarantee truth.

passage:
Dear Sunaina di,
Something awkward happened. Papa forwarded a message to the whole family group saying every house must register on some website by Friday or the electricity will be cut. He sounded completely sure. He even called Chacha to make him do it. I've always thought Papa knows everything about this stuff; he handles all the bills.
But the website address looked strange, and it asked for bank details. I checked the electricity board's real site. Nothing about it, and there was even a warning about fake messages like this one.
I showed Papa at dinner. My voice was shaking. He went quiet, then said, "Hm, let me check," and later deleted the message from the group. He didn't say sorry, but he didn't scold me either.
Is it wrong that I feel proud and embarrassed at the same time?
Nandini

qa.q: What did the website in the message ask for?
qa.a: It asked for bank details.

qa.q: Why does Nandini feel proud and embarrassed at the same time?
qa.a: Nandini was right to check, which feels good, but correcting Papa, who handles all the bills, felt awkward and a little frightening.

qa.q: What made Nandini's approach sensible?
qa.a: Nandini checked the electricity board's real site, found the warning, and showed Papa calmly at dinner instead of arguing in the family group.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when shown the warning?
qa.a: Papa probably felt embarrassed after telling Chacha to register, which may be why he went quiet and deleted it without saying sorry.

grounding: A teenager checks a sure-sounding parent's forwarded message, finds it fake, and awkwardly corrects him.

passage: In his third week as a trainee site engineer, Karthik stood at the base of the scaffolding with a clipboard. Sabina Ma'am, the senior engineer with fifteen years on sites, pointed up. "Check the slab level on the third floor. Skip the harness, it takes too long. We finish today." Karthik knew the safety rule by heart; they had drilled it on day one. His mouth opened, then closed. She was his senior, older than his mother, and everyone greeted her with a little bow. Saying no felt like slapping her. So he climbed without the harness. On the third level a plank shifted under his boot, and he grabbed a pole just in time. He finished the check with his hands shaking. That night he couldn't eat, replaying the moment he had said nothing.

qa.q: What did Sabina Ma'am tell Karthik to skip?
qa.a: She told him to skip the harness because it takes too long.

qa.q: Why did Karthik climb without the harness though he knew the rule?
qa.a: Saying no to a senior everyone bows to felt as rude as slapping her, so respect for rank silenced what he knew.

qa.q: What could Karthik have said at the base of the scaffolding?
qa.a: He could have said politely, 'Ma'am, I'll be quick, but I'll wear the harness,' and if pushed, raised it with the site safety officer that day.

qa.q: How might Karthik's family feel if they knew what happened on the third level?
qa.a: They'd likely be frightened by how close he came, and want him to feel free to refuse unsafe orders.

grounding: A trainee skips a safety harness because his senior told him to and refusing felt disrespectful, and nearly falls.

passage:
Dear Sangeeta,
I need to tell someone, and you're the only one who won't lecture me.
On Friday, Raman sir, the senior partner at the firm, asked me to change the dates on four client invoices so they fall in last quarter. He said it casually, like a small favour. I knew it wasn't right. We studied exactly this in our ethics paper.
But he's been in this business for thirty years and I've been here for three months. Everyone touches his feet at Diwali. How does a trainee say, "Sir, I won't"? So I did it, and said nothing.
I haven't slept properly since. I keep thinking about my name on those files.
This weekend I'm going to talk to my college mentor about what to do now.
Lakshmi

qa.q: What did Raman sir ask Lakshmi to change?
qa.a: He asked Lakshmi to change the dates on four client invoices so they fall in last quarter.

qa.q: Why did Lakshmi go along while knowing it was wrong?
qa.a: Raman sir has thirty years in the business and everyone touches his feet, so refusing felt impossible for a three-month trainee.

qa.q: Is talking to the college mentor a good next step, and why?
qa.a: Yes; a trusted, experienced person can help Lakshmi work out how to raise it properly and what to do next, instead of carrying it alone.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Sangeeta may feel worried for Lakshmi and glad to be trusted, since the letter says Sangeeta won't lecture.

grounding: A trainee changes invoice dates on a senior's instruction because refusing a respected elder felt impossible.

passage: Four months into my hotel kitchen traineeship, I learned something about myself I didn't like, Raghav. Chef Menon, the head chef, a legend, told me one night to mix the gravy that had sat out since morning into the fresh batch for a big party. "Nobody will know. Waste is loss." I'm Vidya, the girl who topped food safety in college. I knew it was wrong. But in that kitchen you say "Yes, Chef" and nothing else. The juniors don't even look him in the eye. So I said "Yes, Chef" and did it. Nobody got sick, thank God. But I waited for a phone call all week. That's when I went to the HR office, shaking, told them what happened, and asked for a transfer. I still can't believe how easy it was to obey.

qa.q: What did Chef Menon tell Vidya to do?
qa.a: He told Vidya to mix the gravy that had sat out since morning into the fresh batch for a big party.

qa.q: Why did Vidya say 'Yes, Chef' despite knowing it was wrong?
qa.a: In that kitchen juniors say 'Yes, Chef' and nothing else, so refusing a legend felt impossible, even for someone who topped food safety.

qa.q: What could Vidya have said in the moment instead?
qa.a: She could have said, 'Chef, I'm worried about food safety; can we check with the manager?' and asked another senior on duty for help.

qa.q: What would change for the party guests if Vidya had spoken up?
qa.a: They would have been served food that hadn't sat out all day, instead of relying on luck.

grounding: A trainee cook obeys a head chef's unsafe instruction because questioning him felt impossible in the kitchen's hierarchy.

passage: Siddharth, you say you can't question your director because you admire him too much. Let me tell you about Mr Lobo. I was twenty-five, a junior engineer, and he was the man I wanted to become. One day he declared that the new bridge pillars needed no extra testing; he'd built fifty bridges. I admired him, and I also had soil reports on my desk that worried me. So I asked, "Sir, how did you decide that? I'd like to learn." He explained. Then I said, "May I show you something from this week's soil tests?" He read them for a long time. We tested. He was right about two pillars and wrong about one. He shook my hand afterwards. Respect him, beta. Just don't hand him your eyes. Your Manoj uncle learned that at twenty-five.

qa.q: What was on young Manoj's desk that worried him?
qa.a: Soil reports on his desk worried him.

qa.q: What does young Manoj's 'I'd like to learn' show about how he felt toward Mr Lobo?
qa.a: He calls him the man he wanted to become and asked, 'I'd like to learn', showing respect even while doubting the claim.

qa.q: What steps from Manoj's story can Siddharth use with his director?
qa.a: Ask how the director reached the claim, then politely offer the evidence, keeping respect for the person separate from the idea.

qa.q: How did Mr Lobo respond to being questioned?
qa.a: Mr Lobo explained, read the reports for a long time, agreed to test, and shook Manoj's hand afterwards.

grounding: An uncle recalls asking, at twenty-five, how an admired senior reached a claim, offering soil data politely, and finding him partly right.

passage: Five minutes before the client walked in, Mohit, the agency's creative head, tapped the storyboard. "Our buyers are mostly retired people. Everyone knows that. Keep the ad slow and serious." Sudha had admired Mohit since her internship; his campaigns were the reason she'd joined. She also had last month's survey open on her tablet. With the clock ticking, she kept it short. "Mohit, can I ask how we got that picture of the buyers? I want to be sure I'm seeing it right." He shrugged. "Twenty years of experience." "That counts for a lot," she said. "This survey shows almost half our buyers are under thirty. Could we add one faster version, just in case?" Mohit squinted at the chart, then sighed. "Fine. Two versions. You present the second." The door opened.

qa.q: What did last month's survey show?
qa.a: Almost half our buyers are under thirty.

qa.q: How does Sudha feel about Mohit while she questions him?
qa.a: She still admires him, since his campaigns were why she joined, but trusts the survey enough to raise it. 🙂

qa.q: Which part of Sudha's approach worked best under the time pressure?
qa.a: Asking how the claim was reached, then offering one chart and a small 'just in case' option, kept it short, respectful and hard to refuse.

qa.q: How might Mohit feel after squinting at the chart?
qa.a: Mohit may feel a little caught out but also respected, since she praised his experience and only asked for a second version.

grounding: Under time pressure, a young professional politely asks how a senior reached a claim, shows data, and keeps her admiration intact.

passage: At a crowded seminar hall in Bengaluru's city planning office, Professor Varun Rao, whose textbook Pema had read three times in college, told the room that cycle lanes never work in Indian cities. "People won't use them. I've studied this for thirty years." Several heads nodded. Pema, twenty-six and eight months into her job, felt her heart speed up. She raised her hand. "Sir, your book is the reason I joined planning," she began. "Could you tell us how that conclusion was reached? I ask because our team counted riders on the new Jayanagar lane last month." She held up a printout: numbers had tripled in a year. Professor Rao studied it. "Interesting. Different from my older studies. Send me the data?" Afterwards a junior colleague whispered, "How did you dare?" Pema smiled. "I didn't argue with him. Just with the idea."

qa.q: What did Pema's team count on the Jayanagar lane?
qa.a: They counted riders on the new Jayanagar lane, and numbers had tripled in a year.

qa.q: What does Pema's speeding heart suggest as she raises her hand?
qa.a: It suggests she felt nervous challenging someone she admired, yet trusted her data enough to speak.

qa.q: How did Pema keep her challenge respectful?
qa.a: She thanked him for his book, asked how he reached the conclusion, and offered her count instead of saying he was wrong.

qa.q: How does the junior colleague see Pema's question?
qa.a: The junior colleague sees it as daring, as if questioning a senior were risky, while Pema sees it as arguing only with the idea.

grounding: A young planner asks a famous professor how he reached a claim and offers new data, respecting him while questioning the idea.

passage:
Week 1. In Zubin's first meeting as front-office lead at the hotel, he suggested moving check-in to a tablet system. Six heads nodded. Nobody asked a single question. By Friday the system was crashing, and he heard in the corridor that Afreen had seen the problem coming.
Week 2. Zubin thought about it on the bus home. When he was a receptionist, he'd never argued with the old manager either. The title did it. So on Monday he opened the meeting differently: "Before I share my idea, tell me what could go wrong with it. I mean it." Silence, then Afreen spoke up about the weak signal in the lobby.
Week 4. Afreen came to his desk with bad news: a double booking for a wedding party. Zubin said, "Thank you for telling me early," and meant it. Two others brought problems that same week.

qa.q: What did Afreen raise when Zubin asked what could go wrong?
qa.a: Afreen spoke up about the weak signal in the lobby.

qa.q: What did Zubin realise on the bus home?
qa.a: He realised his title made people quiet, just as he had never argued with the old manager when he was a receptionist.

qa.q: Why was thanking Afreen for the double booking news important?
qa.a: Thanking Afreen for bad news showed it was safe to speak up, which is why two others brought problems that same week.

qa.q: How might Afreen have felt watching the tablet system crash?
qa.a: Afreen may have felt frustrated and a bit guilty, having seen the problem coming but not feeling able to say so.

grounding: A young lead notices his staff never disagree, realises his title silences them, then invites problems early and thanks bad news.

passage: Anirban, you tell me your team agrees with everything you say. That reminds me of young Tsering, when I worked under him at the tea estate office in Darjeeling. He was twenty-five, the owner's nephew, and every meeting ended in nods. Then one monsoon the drying machine broke, and we all knew it had been making a noise for weeks. Nobody had told him. I still remember his face. He didn't shout. At the next meeting he said, "I'm the owner's nephew, so maybe you're afraid to tell me things. Before I speak, each of you tell me one worry." He started with me. I was so nervous my cup rattled. When I told him about the leaking roof, he said, "Thank you, Dolma-la. This is exactly what I need." After that, we told him everything.

qa.q: What had been making a noise for weeks?
qa.a: The drying machine had been making a noise for weeks.

qa.q: What did Tsering seem to realise after the drying machine broke?
qa.a: He seemed to realise that being the owner's nephew made people afraid to tell him things, so his meetings ended in nods.

qa.q: What could Anirban borrow from Tsering's approach?
qa.a: Anirban could ask each person for one worry before Anirban speaks, and thank whoever brings bad news.

qa.q: How did Dolma feel being asked first for a worry?
qa.a: Dolma was so nervous the cup rattled, but felt valued when Tsering thanked Dolma for the news about the leaking roof.

grounding: An elder recalls a young manager noticing his title silenced staff, asking for worries first and thanking bad news.

passage: The school-bus tracking project was due to the client in two days, and the office generator had failed again, so Rajat held the team meeting by the window in the afternoon heat. "Any concerns about the launch?" he asked. Deepika and Farida looked at their notebooks. Silence. It was always silence. Rajat was about to say, "Great, let's go," when he remembered a line from his last job: if nobody disagrees, you haven't heard the truth yet. He was the founder; of course they didn't want to be the one who slowed him down. So he tried again. "I'll go first. My worry is the rural routes. Now each of you, one worry, and I'll thank you for it." Farida hesitated, then said the tracking failed in the hills during testing. Deepika added that two schools hadn't sent route lists. Rajat wrote both down. "Thank you. That's the most useful thing anyone's said all week."

qa.q: What did Farida say failed in the hills during testing?
qa.a: The tracking failed in the hills during testing.

qa.q: Why did Rajat decide the silence wasn't agreement?
qa.a: He remembered that if nobody disagrees you haven't heard the truth yet, and realised that as founder his staff didn't want to slow him down.

qa.q: Why did going first with his own worry help?
qa.a: Naming his own worry first made it safer for others to share theirs, and promising thanks lowered the risk of speaking.

qa.q: What might it be like for Deepika to report the missing route lists?
qa.a: Deepika might feel nervous about delaying the launch, then relieved when Rajat calls it the most useful thing all week. 🙏

grounding: Under deadline pressure a young founder notices his staff stay silent, goes first with a worry, and thanks them for problems.

passage: At the village anganwadi in Mehatpur, Didi tied red ribbons on half the children and blue on the rest, just for a running game. By lunch, Baljeet had changed. He shared his jaggery only with the red-ribbon children. When Kiran, wearing blue, held out a hand, Baljeet hid the jaggery behind his back. "Blue team is bad," he said. "They cheat." Kiran hadn't even run yet. Didi watched, then swapped two ribbons, Baljeet's included. Now he was blue. He looked at his wrist, puzzled, and slowly held out the jaggery to Kiran.

qa.q: What did Didi tie on the children?
qa.a: Didi tied red ribbons on half the children and blue on the rest.

qa.q: Why does Baljeet say the blue team is bad?
qa.a: Wearing red made the red children feel like his group, so the blue ones suddenly felt like outsiders, though nothing had happened.

qa.q: What did Didi's ribbon swap help Baljeet notice?
qa.a: It showed him the teams were just ribbons, and the child he called bad could be his teammate a moment later.

qa.q: How might Kiran feel when Baljeet hides the jaggery?
qa.a: Kiran might feel hurt and confused, left out because of a ribbon before the game had even started.

grounding: A young boy shares only with his ribbon team and calls the other team bad, until his teacher swaps ribbons.

passage: In the Madrid kindergarten, two classes shared the playground: the Butterflies and the Ladybirds. Tomás was a Butterfly. When Olga, a Ladybird, asked to join his sandcastle, he spread his arms over it. "No Ladybirds. Ladybirds are mean." "Why?" asked Ms Ines. Tomás thought hard. "Because they're Ladybirds." He gave his spade to a Butterfly he'd never played with before. The next week, Ms Ines mixed both classes at one painting table. Tomás sat beside Olga, shared the blue paint, chatted about dogs, and forgot to call anyone mean.

qa.q: Which class was Tomás in?
qa.a: Tomás was a Butterfly.

qa.q: What does 'Because they're Ladybirds' show about Tomás's thinking?
qa.a: It shows he has no real reason; being in the other class is enough to make Olga feel like one of 'them'.

qa.q: How did Ms Ines help without scolding?
qa.a: She mixed both classes at one painting table, so Tomás got to know Olga as a person rather than a Ladybird.

qa.q: What is it like for Olga to be kept away from the sandcastle?
qa.a: Olga is shut out just for being in the other class, which might leave Olga sad and puzzled.

grounding: A young boy blocks a child from the other class and calls them mean only because of the class name.

passage: On sports day at Little Steps preschool, Ankita Ma'am pulled names from a box to make two teams, Tigers and Lions. Ayaan was a Tiger. Within ten minutes he was cheering only for Tigers and booing when Jyoti, a Lion, won the sack race. At snack time he gave his extra biscuits to three Tigers. "Lions are losers," he announced, though the Lions were winning. After snacks, Ankita Ma'am pulled names again for the relay. Ayaan landed on the Lions with Jyoti. He frowned, then shouted "Go Lions!" louder than anyone.

qa.q: How did Ankita Ma'am make the two teams?
qa.a: She pulled names from a box to make two teams, Tigers and Lions.

qa.q: Why does Ayaan call the Lions losers when they are winning?
qa.a: Being a Tiger made the Tigers feel like 'us', so the Lions felt like the other side no matter how they played.

qa.q: How could Ankita Ma'am help Ayaan notice what happened?
qa.a: She could gently remind him how he booed Jyoti earlier and now cheers with her, and ask him how that feels.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel when Ayaan becomes Jyoti's teammate?
qa.a: Jyoti might be surprised, and a bit amused, that the boy who booed Jyoti now shouts 'Go Lions!' louder than anyone. 😅

grounding: A young boy on a randomly drawn team shares only with teammates and calls the other team losers, then switches when redrawn.

passage: Aparna, your cousin is shouting at the TV again, calling the other team cheats for the same tackle his team made. He reminds me of my brother Gopal. At our school in Madurai there were four houses, and Gopal was Green House, heart and soul. On sports day, when a Green runner stepped over the line, Gopal shouted, "Accident! The chalk was faded!" Ten minutes later a Blue boy did the same, and Gopal was on his feet: "Cheating! Disqualify him!" I was in Blue, so we fought all the way home. Amma laughed and said, "Same line, same feet, Gopal." He's seventy now. Last month, on the phone, he admitted Green was probably the worst house for rules. Your Rukmini Paati still remembers that faded chalk.

qa.q: Which house was Gopal in?
qa.a: Gopal was Green House, heart and soul.

qa.q: Why did Gopal call it an accident for Green but cheating for Blue?
qa.a: He loved Green House so much that belonging bent his fairness; his own side's foul felt excusable and the other side's felt wicked.

qa.q: What could Aparna say to the cousin who is shouting at the TV?
qa.a: Aparna could borrow Amma's line and ask, 'Same tackle, same feet?' to help him see he judges the two teams differently.

qa.q: How did young Rukmini, in Blue House, experience Gopal's shouting?
qa.a: Rukmini felt her house was treated unfairly, so they fought all the way home, though now it is a fond memory. 🙂

grounding: A grandmother recalls her brother excusing his house's foul but calling the same act cheating by another house.

passage: Rain had been threatening all afternoon, and the house cricket final had to finish before the sky opened. Kamal, captain of Tagore House, was fielding at point when his own bowler, Nikhil, threw the ball instead of bowling it. Kamal clapped. "Great ball!" Four overs later, with thunder rumbling, Arohi of Raman House did exactly the same. Kamal flung down his cap. "That's a throw! Cheating! Umpire!" The PT sir raised an eyebrow. "Kamal, Nikhil's arm bent the same way." "That was different, sir. It was wet, the ball slipped." "And now?" Kamal opened his mouth. The first fat drops of rain fell, and everyone ran for the corridor, but Arohi looked back at him, arms folded, until he looked away.

qa.q: What did Kamal do when Arohi threw the ball?
qa.a: Kamal flung down his cap and shouted, 'That's a throw! Cheating! Umpire!'

qa.q: Why did Nikhil's throw seem fine to Kamal but Arohi's seem like cheating?
qa.a: As Tagore House captain, Kamal wanted his side to win, so he found an excuse for Nikhil and none for the rival house.

qa.q: What could Kamal do after he looks away from Arohi?
qa.a: He could admit to PT sir and Arohi that both throws were the same, and use one rule for both houses.

qa.q: What might Arohi be thinking, arms folded, looking back at Kamal?
qa.a: Arohi probably thinks Kamal is being unfair, calling out the same action that Kamal clapped for from Tagore House.

grounding: A house captain cheers his own bowler's illegal throw and calls the same action cheating from a rival, as rain rushes the match.

passage: The inter-house kabaddi match in the school's concrete courtyard in Pune was the loudest event of the year. Yogesh, in Shivaji House, had painted his cheeks orange. When Shivaji's raider stepped out of bounds and kept going, Yogesh screamed, "He was in! He was in!" When the Tilak raider did the same a minute later, Yogesh was first to shout, "Out! Out! Cheat!" His classmate Swati, who was in Tilak and standing beside him, stared. "It's the same line, Yogesh." "Our raider was fast. The line is blurry there." "And ours?" "Yours was cheating." He said it with a grin, carried along by the chanting. On the bus home he noticed the orange paint on his fingers and didn't feel so sure any more.

qa.q: What colour had Yogesh painted his cheeks?
qa.a: Orange.

qa.q: Why does Yogesh say 'Our raider was fast. The line is blurry there'?
qa.a: He wants his house to win so badly that he finds excuses for Shivaji House while calling the same step cheating from Tilak.

qa.q: How could a teacher help students judge fairly during house matches?
qa.a: A teacher could replay both raids side by side and ask students to call them without knowing which house was which.

qa.q: How might Swati feel standing beside Yogesh?
qa.a: Swati may feel frustrated and a bit hurt that Swati's house is called cheats for the same step Yogesh defended.

grounding: A boy cheers his house's out-of-bounds raid but calls the same move by another house cheating.
